name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_SEQ_Q01 - Sequence of hypothalamic control over anterior pituitary

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events in the correct chronological sequence for the regulation of anterior pituitary hormone secretion by the hypothalamus:

  • P: Transport of hypothalamic hormones through the portal circulatory system
  • Q: Synthesis of releasing or inhibiting hormones by hypothalamic neurosecretory cells (nuclei)
  • R: Stimulation or inhibition of hormone synthesis and secretion in the anterior pituitary
  • S: Passage of hormones through axons and release from hypothalamic nerve endings

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The hypothalamus regulates the anterior pituitary via neurohormones transported through a specialised portal circulatory system.

Step 2: Chronological Ordering of Events
First, groups of neurosecretory cells called nuclei in the hypothalamus synthesise releasing hormones (such as GnRH) or inhibiting hormones (such as somatostatin). Next, these hormones travel down the hypothalamic axons and are released from their nerve endings. They then enter and travel through the portal circulatory system to reach the anterior pituitary. Finally, they act on the anterior pituitary cells to stimulate or inhibit the synthesis and secretion of pituitary hormones.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is synthesis in hypothalamic nuclei, axonal passage and release from nerve endings, transport via the portal circulatory system, and regulation of anterior pituitary secretion (Q → S → P → R).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_SEQ_Q02 - Sequence of protein hormone action via second messengers

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps in the correct sequential order for the mechanism of action of a protein hormone such as follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) on an ovarian target cell:

  • P: Generation of a second messenger such as cyclic AMP or \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\)
  • Q: Binding of FSH to a specific membrane-bound receptor on the ovarian cell membrane
  • R: Physiological responses such as ovarian growth
  • S: Biochemical responses regulating cellular metabolism

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Protein hormones such as FSH do not enter the target cell; instead, they act through membrane-bound receptors and intracellular second messengers.

Step 2: Chronological Ordering of Events
Initially, FSH binds to its specific receptor located on the ovarian cell membrane to form a hormone-receptor complex. This binding triggers the generation of second messengers such as cyclic AMP or \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) inside the cell. The second messengers then initiate a cascade of biochemical responses that regulate cellular metabolism. Ultimately, these cumulative biochemical changes produce physiological responses such as ovarian growth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological order is membrane receptor binding, second messenger generation, biochemical responses, and physiological responses (Q → P → S → R).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_SEQ_Q03 - Sequence of steroid hormone action via nuclear receptors

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events in the correct chronological sequence for the mechanism of action of a steroid hormone such as estrogen on a uterine target cell:

  • P: Interaction of the hormone-receptor complex with the genome
  • Q: Entry of estrogen across the uterine cell membrane into the target cell
  • R: Synthesis of mRNA and proteins leading to tissue growth and differentiation
  • S: Binding of estrogen to an intracellular nuclear receptor to form a hormone-receptor complex

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Steroid hormones (such as estrogen, cortisol, testosterone, and progesterone) interact with intracellular, mostly nuclear receptors to regulate gene expression.

Step 2: Chronological Ordering of Events
First, estrogen passes across the uterine cell membrane to enter the target cell. Inside the nucleus, it binds to its specific intracellular nuclear receptor, forming a hormone-receptor complex. This hormone-receptor complex then interacts directly with the genome (DNA) to regulate gene expression or chromosome function. Finally, transcription of mRNA and translation into proteins occur, resulting in cumulative biochemical actions and physiological responses such as tissue growth and differentiation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is entry across the cell membrane, binding to the nuclear receptor, interaction with the genome, and mRNA/protein synthesis leading to tissue growth and differentiation (Q → S → P → R).
